hints: Think about what a voltmeter connected between two half cells is actually measuring.
Recall the three standard condition values for temperature, pressure of gases and concentration of ions that make any E value a standard value.
walkthrough:
Picture what E(cell) compares**
Imagine two different half cells joined together. Each one has its own tendency to gain or lose electrons. When you connect them, electrons flow and you read a voltage. That voltage, the difference between the two half cell potentials, is the cell potential.

Add the word standard**
Standard simply means measured in a fair, agreed state so values can be compared. For A Level that is always $T = 298\ \text{K}$, any gas at $p = 1\ \text{atm}$ ($101\ \text{kPa}$) and every ion solution at $c = 1\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$. Put both ideas together for the full definition.

Final answer: The potential difference between two half-cells / electrodes in an electrochemical cell.
Measured under standard conditions: temperature $298\ \text{K}$, pressure $1\ \text{atm}$ for gases, all solutions of concentration $1\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$.

hints: Remember that any standard electrode potential is measured against the same reference electrode, the standard hydrogen electrode.
Think about what components a hydrogen half cell needs besides solution, and what a $\text{Pb}^{2+}/\text{Pb}$ half cell needs besides solution.
Recall how the two separate beakers must be joined electrically without mixing, and how the potential difference is measured.
Check that every chemical is at standard concentration and gas pressure, and that each electrode material is correctly chosen for its half cell.
walkthrough:
Set up the reference side**
You are measuring $\text{Pb}^{2+}/\text{Pb}$ against hydrogen, so one side must be the standard hydrogen electrode. That is a Pt electrode, which is inert and just conducts electrons, dipping into $1\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)}$, for example $\text{HCl}$, with $\text{H}_{2}$ gas at $1\ \text{atm}$ bubbled continuously over the Pt surface. Draw a gas delivery tube with in and out.

Set up the test side**
The other side is much simpler. It is a metal, metal ion electrode. Place a Pb rod into a solution containing $\text{Pb}^{2+}\text{(aq)}$, for example $\text{Pb(NO}_{3})_{2}$, at $1\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$.

Complete the circuit correctly**
The two electrolytes must not mix but ions must be able to move, so join the beakers with a salt bridge, typically filter paper soaked in $\text{KNO}_{3}$. Join the Pb and Pt electrodes with wires through a high resistance voltmeter to read $E$ without drawing current.

Label everything for standard conditions**
Label $\text{H}_{2}$, Pt, $\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)}$, $\text{Pb}$, $\text{Pb}^{2+}\text{(aq)}$, salt bridge and V. Standard means both solutions $1\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ and $\text{H}_{2}$ at $1\ \text{atm}$ and $298\ \text{K}$.

Final answer: Left beaker: Pt electrode in $1\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)}$ with $\text{H}_{2}$ gas at $1\ \text{atm}$ bubbled over it via inlet and outlet. Right beaker: Pb electrode in $1\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{Pb}^{2+}\text{(aq)}$. The two solutions joined by a salt bridge, electrodes joined via a voltmeter.

hints: Write the reduction equilibrium for the lead electrode: $\text{Pb}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \leftrightharpoons \text{Pb}$ and think which side is favoured if $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ is removed.
Link a decreased tendency to reduce to the sign of E, remembering $E^{\ominus} = -0.13\ \text{V}$ is already negative.
walkthrough:
See the equilibrium behind E**
An electrode potential reflects the position of $$\text{Pb}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{e}^{-} \leftrightharpoons \text{Pb(s)}$$ If reduction goes well to the right, E is more positive. If it lies to the left, E is more negative.

Apply Le Chatelier**
Dilute the $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ ions. You have removed a reactant from the left. The system opposes the change by shifting left to try to make more $\text{Pb}^{2+}$. That means $\text{Pb}$ is more likely to oxidise than $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ is to reduce. The electrode becomes even less reducing-friendly than standard, so starting from $-0.13\ \text{V}$ it moves to a more negative value.

Final answer: Tick: more negative.
Lowering $[\text{Pb}^{2+}]$ shifts the equilibrium $\text{Pb}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{e}^{-} \leftrightharpoons \text{Pb(s)}$ to the left, reduction is less favoured, so $E$ becomes more negative.

hints: Start from $Q = It$ and remember to convert the 80 minutes into seconds before multiplying by $0.40\ \text{A}$.
Use the given half equation to find the mole ratio of electrons to Pb, then convert moles of Pb to mass using $A_{r} = 207.2$.
walkthrough:
Find the total charge passed**
Charge is current times time in seconds: $$Q = It$$ So $$Q = 0.40\ \text{A} \times (80 \times 60)\ \text{s} = 0.40 \times 4800 = 1920\ \text{C}$$ This is the total push of electrons delivered.

Convert charge to mass of lead**
One mole of electrons carries $96500\ \text{C}$. Moles of electrons: $$n(\text{e}^{-}) = 1920 / 96500 = 0.0199\ \text{mol}$$ From $$\text{Pb(s)} + \text{SO}_{4}^{2-}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{PbSO}_{4}\text{(s)} + 2\text{e}^{-}$$ $2\ \text{mol e}^{-}$ come from $1\ \text{mol Pb}$, so $$n(\text{Pb}) = 0.0199/2 = 9.95 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$$ Then $$m = n \times A_{r} = 9.95 \times 10^{-3} \times 207.2 \approx 2.06\ \text{g} \approx 2.1\ \text{g}$$

hints: The positive plate $\text{PbO}_{2}$ is reduced to $\text{PbSO}_{4}$, so balance O atoms with $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ and then H atoms with $\text{H}^{+}$ before balancing charge with electrons.
walkthrough:
Balance the reduction at Pb(IV) to Pb(II)**
Lead goes from $+4$ in $\text{PbO}_{2}$ to $+2$ in $\text{PbSO}_{4}$, a gain of $2\text{e}^{-}$. The two O atoms in $\text{PbO}_{2}$ need $4\text{H}^{+}$ to make $2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$, and $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ supplies the sulfate. Check atoms and charge: left $4(+1) -2 -2 = 0$, right $0$. So: $$\text{PbO}_{2}\text{(s)} + \text{SO}_{4}^{2-}\text{(aq)} + 4\text{H}^{+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{PbSO}_{4}\text{(s)} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$

hints: Compare a sealed battery where all chemicals are inside the case with a fuel cell where gases are piped in from outside.
Think about what happens to $[\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}]$ and solid $\text{PbO}_{2}$ / Pb as discharge continues, versus what happens to $[\text{H}_{2}]$ and $[\text{O}_{2}]$ if supply never stops.
walkthrough:
Why the lead-acid voltage drops**
A lead-acid cell is a closed store. Discharge consumes solid Pb, solid $\text{PbO}_{2}$ and $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}\text{(aq)}$ to make solid $\text{PbSO}_{4}$ and water. As acid concentration falls and active solids are coated with sulfate, the cell reaction is less favoured and internal resistance rises, so after several hours the voltage collapses.

Why the fuel cell voltage holds steady**
A $\text{H}_{2}/\text{O}_{2}$ fuel cell is an open flow system. $\text{H}_{2}$ and $\text{O}_{2}$ are fed in continuously from external tanks and product water is removed. Reactant concentrations at the electrodes never deplete, so the electrode potentials and hence the cell voltage stay constant as long as fuel is supplied.

Final answer: Lead-acid cell: reagents $\text{PbO}_{2}$, Pb and $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ are used up / $[\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}]$ decreases, so voltage falls after several hours.
Fuel cell: $\text{H}_{2}$ / $\text{O}_{2}$ fuel is continuously supplied and does not run out, so concentration stays constant and voltage remains constant.
